Right: a narrow range of tolerance is part of a narrow niche.

why.correct: Recovery speed comes from reproductive traits.
options: Right: late breeding and few offspring explain slow recovery.

why.correct: K-selected species can sustain only light harvests.

why.correct: r-selected: many, small, little care, early, short-lived.
options: These are K-selected traits.

Few offspring and a long life are K-selected traits.

options: That would describe species richness, not biotic potential.

why.correct: Name the r-selected traits, then the rebound.

options: Right: K-selected species invest heavily in each offspring.

Habitat range is not what makes K-selected species vulnerable.

why.correct: Weeds that colonize bare ground are classic r-selected species.
options: K-selected plants, such as oaks, grow slowly and reproduce late.

Plants have reproductive strategies too; trees and weeds differ greatly.
No parental care is an r-selected trait.

why.correct: r and K are ends of a range; many species mix traits.
options: Their long life and late breeding are K-selected traits.

Generalist describes niche width, not reproductive strategy.

why.correct: A disruption that hits both an r-selected pest and its slower-breeding predator favors the pest.
options: Birds that raise few young a year recover more slowly than insects.

why.correct: A steep early drop means most of the young die.

why.correct: Lowering deaths at young ages keeps the curve high longer.

options: Right: 950 of 1,000 die in the first year, then survival is high.

why.correct: Deaths over the starting number, times 100: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1{,}000 - 50}{1{,}000} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 95\%</annotation></semantics></math>.

options: The number dying falls each year (500, 250, 125 ...); the fraction stays the same.

why.correct: Survivors at 4 over survivors at 2, times 100: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>62</mn><mn>250</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>24.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{62}{250} \times 100 = 24.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>, about a quarter, as two halvings predict.

why.correct: Type I high then late drop; Type II steady; Type III early drop. Only the log scale statement is correct.
